subject: Biology
title: The 5-Step Decomposition Pathway
quickSummary: Decomposition: Stepwise enzymatic degradation of dead organic detritus into simple inorganic minerals. 5 sequential steps: (1) Fragmentation (detritivores like earthworms break detritus into smaller particles); (2) Leaching (water-soluble inorganic nutrients percolate into soil horizons); (3) Catabolism (extracellular bacterial & fungal saprophytic enzymes digest polymers); (4) Humification (accumulation of dark, amorphous, colloidal Humus); (5) Mineralization (complete microbial breakdown of humus releasing free mineral ions like Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, NH4+).

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Detritus undergoes a 5-step degradation: physical fragmentation by detritivores, downward leaching of soluble minerals, enzymatic catabolism by microbes, humification producing resistant humus, and mineralization releasing inorganic nutrients.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
THE FIVE DECOMPOSITION STEPS
                                    │
  1. FRAGMENTATION ──► Detritivores (Earthworms) break detritus into small particles.
  2. LEACHING      ──► Water-soluble inorganic nutrients sink into soil horizons.
  3. CATABOLISM    ──► Bacterial & fungal enzymes digest complex organic polymers.
  4. HUMIFICATION  ──► Formation of dark, amorphous, resistant Humus.
  5. MINERALIZATION──► Microbial breakdown of humus to release inorganic mineral ions.
conceptBreakdown.content:
### 4.1 Definition of Detritus & Decomposition
- **Detritus**: Dead organic raw material of an ecosystem, including fallen leaves, bark, withered flowers, dead animal carcasses, and fecal matter.
- **Decomposition**: The oxygen-requiring, biological breakdown of complex organic macromolecules in detritus into simple inorganic nutrients ($\text{CO}_2, \text{H}_2\text{O}, \text{NO}_3^-, \text{PO}_4^{3-}$).

### 4.2 Stepwise Decomposition Cascade Matrix

1. **Step 1: Fragmentation**:
   - **Agents**: **Detritivores** (*Earthworms [Eisenia fetida], Termites, Millipedes, Woodlice*).
   - **Mechanism**: Physical chewing, pulverization, and ingestion of coarse detrital litter into tiny fragmented particles, expanding surface area for microbial enzymes.

2. **Step 2: Leaching**:
   - **Agent**: Percolating rain and soil moisture.
   - **Mechanism**: Highly water-soluble inorganic nutrients (e.g., nitrates, soluble sugars, phosphates) dissolve and wash down into lower sub-surface soil horizons, precipitating as unavailable mineral salts.

3. **Step 3: Catabolism**:
   - **Agents**: Extracellular enzymes secreted by **saprophytic Bacteria and Fungi** (*Aspergillus, Penicillium, Trichoderma*).
   - **Mechanism**: True biochemical digestion: cellulases, pectinases, chitinases, and proteases hydrolyze complex structural polymers into simple inorganic and organic building blocks.
   - *Note*: Fragmentation, Leaching, and Catabolism operate **simultaneously** on detritus.

4. **Step 4: Humification**:
   - **Output**: Accumulation of **Humus**—a dark brown, amorphous, colloidal substance.
   - **Biochemical Properties of Humus**:
     - Extremely resistant to microbial degradation (undergoes degradation at an exceptionally slow rate).
     - Acts as an immense colloidal nutrient reservoir (high Cation Exchange Capacity - CEC).
     - Substantially enhances soil water-holding capacity and aeration.

5. **Step 5: Mineralization**:
   - **Mechanism**: Specialized soil microorganisms slowly catabolize the resistant humus matrix, releasing free **inorganic mineral ions** ($\text{Ca}^{2+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{K}^+, \text{NH}_4^+, \text{SO}_4^{2-}$) directly into the soil solution for root reabsorption.

conceptBreakdown.heading: Soil Horizon Pedogenesis
conceptBreakdown.title: Soil Horizon Pedogenesis
conceptBreakdown.content: Decomposition structures distinct soil horizons: O-Horizon (organic fresh detritus/litter), A-Horizon (topsoil rich in dark humified organic matter and roots), B-Horizon (subsoil accumulating leached minerals), C-Horizon (weathered parent rock), and R-Horizon (bedrock).

conceptBreakdown.heading: C:N Ratio in Decomposition Kinetics
conceptBreakdown.title: C:N Ratio in Decomposition Kinetics
conceptBreakdown.content: Substrates with low Carbon-to-Nitrogen ratios (C:N < 20:1, such as legume foliage) decompose rapidly with immediate net nitrogen mineralization; substrates with high C:N ratios (>50:1, like sawdust) immobilize nitrogen, slowing decomposition.
